title: The New Utilities: Private Power, Social Infrastructure, and the Revival of the Public Utility Concept
pub: Cardozo Law Review, vol. 39, no. 5, p. 1621 (2018)
author: K. Sabeel Rahman

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: Rahman addresses regulation of infrastructural private power, not legal AI’s task-level capabilities, verification requirements, labour effects, or operating-model redesign. The source therefore provides insufficient evidence to determine a position on the cluster proposition.

st.t: Platform governance: External innovation preserves gatekeeper power
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s core account of platforms as privately controlled infrastructure with gatekeeper power, while materially extending it through a public-utility framework for identifying and remedying that power. It acknowledges platform benefits but argues that consolidated control enables rent extraction and control over exchange; its contribution remains conceptual rather than a detailed regulatory programme.
qs: The benefits of platforms depend on consolidated control-but platform power presents another form of problematic private power with outsized abilities to set the terms of exchange, influencing wages, prices, and standards, and extracting rents in the process.
This Part suggests that the public utility framework developed in this Article can help identify and remedy a unique set of problems arising from these firms' position as infrastructural.

kp.k: Infrastructure control, not size alone, warrants heightened oversight
kp.d: Rahman proposes a normative framework for regulating concentrated private power over essential services, rather than an empirical account of AI or legal-services restructuring. Drawing on Progressive Era thought, finance, broadband, and online platforms, he argues that infrastructural importance and users’ dependence matter more than firm size alone. The framework targets access, fairness, accountability, and inequality beyond consumer prices or economic efficiency.
qs: The issue is not necessarily firm size or market share (though these may of course be relevant factors).

Rather, the inquiry encompasses questions about the essential nature of the good or service itself, as well as the capacity of the providers to exert undue influence through their control of the good.

kp.k: Three overlapping conditions identify infrastructural goods
kp.d: Rahman identifies production economies, downstream uses, and necessity-related vulnerability as overlapping conditions warranting heightened scrutiny. Scale and network effects can favor concentration; infrastructure supports many other activities; restricted access can create exploitation and unequal opportunities. This is a contextual diagnostic framework, not a fixed industry classification or measured threshold.
qs: We can therefore define firms and sectors that might warrant greater regulatory oversight by examining three overlapping conditions: the economics of production; the downstream uses of the good or service; and the degree to which the good or service is a necessity that makes its users particularly vulnerable to exploitation.
Social infrastructure connotes the category of goods and services that enable a wide array of downstream uses for individuals and communities.

kp.k: Infrastructure status changes with technology and social dependence
kp.d: The author argues that goods can become infrastructural as technologies, production arrangements, and social expectations change. Broadband illustrates a service moving from luxury toward necessity. Classification therefore requires ongoing, context-specific judgment rather than mechanical application of historical utility categories.
qs: It is also important to note that these sets of infrastructural goods are not static.
Technological and social change over time can move goods into and out of any one of these categories.

kp.k: Public utility complements antitrust and corporate governance
kp.d: Rahman presents public utility, antitrust, and corporate governance as historically complementary responses to private power. He argues that governance mechanisms struggle to represent dispersed publics dependent on infrastructure, while breaking up providers can sacrifice useful integration and scale. He does not reject antitrust generally: utility tools may remain necessary even when firm-size restrictions are appropriate.
qs: Corporate governance is of limited efficacy in addressing private power concerns when it comes to infrastructural goods.
Antitrust law similarly has difficulties in addressing the problems of private power over infrastructural goods.

Furthermore, there is the difficulty that shareholders by definition do not have the same interests or aspirations as citizens: what we want as consumers or investors is not necessarily the same thing as what we want as a public.

kp.k: Firewalls separate essential services from conflicting activities
kp.d: The first regulatory strategy restricts combinations of activities, corporate structures, or adjacent businesses that can contaminate essential services with risk, self-dealing, or discrimination. Examples include separating banking functions from risky trading and separating platform infrastructure from competing proprietary products. Rahman treats structural restraints as potentially preferable when complexity or capture undermines ongoing discretionary supervision.
qs: First, regulations might focus on creating firewalls: restrictions on the activities and powers of firms that provide these infrastructural goods and services that limit a commingling of business models.
Relatedly, firewalls might take the form of legally imposed limits on corporate structure.

kp.k: Public obligations protect access and underserved constituencies
kp.d: The second strategy imposes context-specific obligations on infrastructural providers: nondiscrimination, fair pricing, service to all comers, and potentially affirmative provision to underserved communities. These are proposed regulatory duties arising from the public importance of the service, not claims that all identified platforms already bear such duties.
qs: A second regulatory strategy involves the imposition of public obligations on infrastructural firms.
Depending on the industry and public concerns, other affirmative obligations might also be required, for example, to serve underserved areas or constituencies.
The exact requirements would necessarily have to be tailored according to the context.

kp.k: Public options combine provision, accountability, and competitive pressure
kp.d: The third strategy uses publicly chartered providers to supply basic services, reach excluded users, and place price and quality pressure on private providers. Rahman distinguishes public options competing alongside private firms from exclusive public provision. Their proposed accountability operates through both political voice and users’ ability to choose an alternative.
qs: A third regulatory strategy involves state-chartered providers for these infrastructural goods or services, providing a kind of public option.
At the extreme, the public option may be an exclusive one-in other words, setting up the state as the sole provider of the good, through government owned and operated vehicles.
A lesser version of this would see the public option compete alongside private providers.

kp.k: Historical utility failures inform flexible regulatory design
kp.d: Rahman acknowledges historical difficulties with judicial definitions of public interest and reasonable rates, regulatory capture, higher costs, and overinvestment incentives. He attributes these problems principally to particular institutional implementations rather than the underlying utility concept. His recommendation is adaptive administrative regulation and structural safeguards, not wholesale restoration of historical rate-setting regimes.
qs: The legacy of the public utility era was decidedly mixed.
Indeed, this Article does not suggest, and is not meant to suggest, that we should mechanically copy and reinstate old models of public utility regulation.
It does not offer a blueprint for public policy-many details would have to be subsequently worked out to apply any one of these strategies in a particular policy context.

kp.k: Net neutrality illustrates adapted utility regulation
kp.d: Rahman interprets the FCC’s net-neutrality initiatives, especially the 2015 Open Internet Order, as adapted public-utility regulation protecting data transmission from blocking, throttling, and prioritization. He emphasizes Title II reclassification combined with forbearance from more stringent obligations. Municipal broadband illustrates public options, although the article records the Sixth Circuit’s August 2016 reversal of the FCC’s municipal broadband decision and the subsequent rollback of net neutrality; these examples are historically situated, not statements of present law.
qs: The 2015 Order holds that ISPs can no longer block, slow-down ("throttle"), prioritize, or otherwise interfere with internet traffic.

In imposing common carrier obligations, the FCC was sure to provide a safety valve where it would exempt ISPs from some of the more stringent forms of common carrier and rate regulation burdens through a "forbearance" regime.
Furthermore, the municipal broadband decision was overturned by the Sixth Circuit by August 2016.

kp.k: Financial reform applies utility principles through multiple proposals
kp.d: The article treats banking as foundational infrastructure historically supported by public guarantees. It groups financial-reform proposals into firewalls, public service obligations, and public banking options, including product approval, restrictions on proprietary trading and holding-company structures, postal banking, and narrow banking. These proposals vary substantially: Ricks emphasizes panic-proofing money-like instruments, while Levitin proposes separating deposit and lending functions. Rahman explicitly cautions that regulatory complexity, industry influence, and political rollback threaten implementation.
qs: Finance represents another kind of infrastructural good, a critical service upon which the entire economy depends.

One approach to regulating modern finance involves the strategy of firewalling: cordoning off the core, essential service from other riskier or potentially exploitative uses, and limiting the types of firms and activities that can operate in this domain.
These proposals are not necessarily guaranteed to succeed; as financial regulation literature  explores in great detail, financial regulation is extremely difficult to implement.

kp.k: Information platforms create power beyond privacy risks
kp.d: Rahman argues that Google and Facebook function as information infrastructure whose control over distribution can produce exclusion, manipulation, and discrimination. He distinguishes deliberate intervention from biased outcomes emerging through algorithms without intentional wrongdoing. He reports and extends other scholars’ proposals, including Balkin’s information fiduciaries and Pasquale’s nondiscrimination approach, recommending consideration of separation, search neutrality, and public alternatives rather than privacy protection alone.
qs: But this creates a vulnerability among users who could be excluded from access, or, more troublingly, may be consuming a tainted or manipulated information stream.
Indeed, the problems of discrimination, manipulation, misinformation, and the like inhere in the very business model and structure of platforms themselves.
Firewalls might help by separating out the branded services offered by these firms from the conduit function that they also serve.
Similarly, we might require a form of "search neutrality," equivalent to the common carriage, nondiscrimination principles developed in the net neutrality context.

kp.k: Amazon combines infrastructure provision with competing commercial interests
kp.d: Rahman characterizes Amazon as retail, shipping, and logistics infrastructure rather than simply a search portal or bookseller. Its simultaneous role as platform operator and proprietary retailer motivates proposed limits on vertical integration and nondiscrimination obligations. These are structural recommendations intended to prevent infrastructure dominance from extending into adjacent businesses, not findings that a specified intervention has succeeded.
qs: But Amazon is more than just a search portal.
For example, prophylactic limits on vertical integration by platforms like Amazon could limit the spillover of dominance in retail logistics to adjacent lines of business

Similarly, public obligations like nondiscrimination realized through platform neutrality regulations could apply just as readily to Amazon in its capacity as retail platform, as it does to informational platforms like Google.

kp.k: Uber and Airbnb remain conditional utility candidates
kp.d: Rahman distinguishes these potentially emergent utilities from more entrenched infrastructural platforms. Network effects and accumulated user data may make competition difficult, while integration into transport, housing, or delivery could increase public dependence. However, he explicitly questions whether their services qualify as necessities and favors facilitating competition where feasible. Possible responses include franchise-linked public obligations, data-enabled enforcement, public digital intermediaries, and worker-owned alternatives; their effectiveness remains prospective.
qs: But it is unclear to what extent these services are "necessities" warranting a full- blown public utility treatment.

If genuine competition remains a possibility, it may be preferable to facilitate new market entrants rather than  ratifying  Uber  and Airbnb's  dominance  and  imposing corresponding utility-style regulations.
This tipping point for triggering public utility regulations may not have been reached yet-whether or not it is would be a matter of judgment and context-but the potential is very much there.

kp.k: Regulatory capacity and organized constituencies remain necessary
kp.d: Although structural safeguards reduce reliance on continuous expert supervision, Rahman argues that agencies still need technical competence and enforcement capacity, particularly for nondiscrimination. He also attributes the emergence and durability of reforms partly to civil-society organization, citing sustained advocacy around net neutrality. Public-utility policy therefore requires institutional resources and political support, not simply an analytically attractive framework.
qs: That said, there will still be a need to ensure a baseline level of expertise and capacity to manage these public utility regulatory strategies, particularly when it comes to the need to enforce public obligations such as nondiscrimination requirements.
The technical needs here, while doable, would require notable changes to regulatory agency structures and staff.
Indeed, the FCC's net neutrality regime in part resulted from sustained social movement organizing and pressure on the FCC; it was not just a product of presidential influence or agency expertise.

kp.k: Lawyers contribute institutional design and interdisciplinary translation
kp.d: The article’s direct implication for the legal profession concerns lawyers’ public-facing role in regulatory design, not AI-driven changes to legal tasks, staffing, billing, or training. Rahman argues that lawyers have distinctive expertise in accountability and institutional design, and describes their role bridging technical experts, political actors, and policymakers during the net-neutrality debate. He calls for comparable contributions in finance and the internet economy.
qs: The concerns raised by this Article-focused on problems of power, accountability, and institutional design-are areas where law and lawyers have particular expertise to contribute, distinct from but complementary to the work done by more quantitative, formal, and empirical scholars in economics.

Indeed, in the net neutrality battle, lawyers played a critical role bridging the gaps between technologists with deep understandings of how the internet works, political figures facing constituent and interest group pressures, and the policymakers charged with formulating a regulatory regime that would address the central public needs in an effective way.
These questions of regulatory system design suggest an important public-facing role for the future of business law, regulatory theory, and the legal profession.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Rahman makes cross-domain claims about algorithmic platforms and infrastructure regulation, not predictions about AI automating legal services.
pts.d: Rahman argues that platforms concentrate private control over access to information, commerce and services. Algorithmic matching can improve efficiency, but platform control also creates opportunities for extraction, manipulation and discrimination. These harms can emerge without intentional programmer misconduct. He proposes adapting public utility strategies—firewalls, public obligations and public options—to constrain this power while preserving technological benefits. Regarding the legal profession, he identifies a growing need for lawyers to bridge technical knowledge, politics and regulatory design; this is a claim about lawyers' regulatory role, not AI-driven substitution of legal work.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence is historical, doctrinal and secondary-source-based, rather than original AI performance or legal-services research.
pts.d: Rahman draws on Progressive Era regulatory history, net-neutrality litigation and FCC policies, financial regulation, platform scholarship and journalism. For algorithmic discrimination he cites work including Cathy O'Neil, Joshua Kroll and colleagues, and Solon Barocas and Andrew Selbst. He reports a search-manipulation study by Robert Epstein and Ronald Robertson concerning influence on undecided voters; this is cited evidence, not Rahman's own experiment or a demonstrated effect on an actual election. His proposed regulatory benefits are arguments informed by these cases and authorities, not measured outcomes from an implemented platform public-utility regime.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Claims concern the platform economy around publication in 2018; future developments are conditional and have no fixed forecast horizon.
pts.d: Rahman treats Google, Facebook and Amazon as already infrastructural, while describing Uber and Airbnb as possible emergent utilities. Heightened regulation depends on scale effects, downstream uses and vulnerability from restricted access—not size alone. He expressly leaves open whether Uber and Airbnb are necessities and whether competition could constrain them. Public or cooperative alternatives would need comparable technology and user experience. Regulatory proposals require contextual design, administrative capacity and political support; the article disclaims providing a finished policy blueprint.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: Affected groups include platform users, businesses dependent on platforms, workers, marginalized communities, regulators and lawyers.
pts.d: Information users may encounter manipulated or discriminatory content streams. Retailers and content providers depend on search visibility and fair platform access. Drivers, riders, hosts and guests face platform control over matching, prices and conditions. Minority and underserved communities may experience discriminatory access or exclusion. Proposed public obligations and alternative platforms seek fair access, better labor conditions and competitive pressure. Regulators would need technical expertise and staffing changes, while lawyers would contribute institutional and regulatory design expertise. The article does not predict changes to law-firm staffing, legal fees or demand for AI-enabled legal services.
